theme: The foolishness of the cross; wisdom from above
readingInstruction: Read 1 Corinthians 1:1-2:16. Paul begins his letter to a gifted but divided church. Notice how he answers pride and division with the cross. Pay particular attention to 1:18-31 and 2:1-5.
settingTheScene: Corinth was a wealthy, cosmopolitan port city in Greece, known for commerce, sensuality, and a love of rhetoric. Paul planted the church around AD 50 during an eighteen-month stay (Acts 18). By AD 55 he writes from Ephesus in response to reports and a letter from the church. They had problems: factions around favorite leaders, moral scandal, lawsuits, confusion about marriage, abuse of the Lord’s Supper, disorder in worship, and doubts about the resurrection. First Corinthians is a letter for a messy church, and so it is very relevant. Paul’s answer to every problem is Christ and him crucified.
observation: “The word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God” (1:18).
“We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles” (1:23).
“For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men” (1:25).
“He is the source of your life in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1:30).
“Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1:31).
“For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified” (2:2).
“These things God has revealed to us through the Spirit” (2:10).
“But we have the mind of Christ” (2:16).
interpretation:
Paul greets the church as “sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints.” Despite their failings, they belong to God. He thanks God for the grace given them: they are enriched in speech and knowledge, lacking in no gift, waiting for the revealing of Christ. Then he turns to the first problem: quarrels. “I appeal to you, brothers… that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you.” Some said, “I follow Paul,” others, “I follow Apollos,” others Cephas, others Christ. “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?”

His answer is the cross. “The word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.” The world seeks signs and wisdom, but “we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.” The message that seems weak and foolish is God’s chosen method. “The foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.”

Look at who you are, he says. Not many were wise, powerful, or of noble birth. “God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong.” So that no one might boast in the presence of God. “He is the source of your life in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption.” Christ is everything. “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

In chapter 2, Paul describes his own ministry. He did not come with lofty speech or wisdom. “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.” He came in weakness and much trembling, and his message was not in plausible words of wisdom but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, “that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.”

Yet there is a wisdom to be spoken among the mature: not the wisdom of this age, but God’s secret and hidden wisdom, decreed before the ages for our glory. None of the rulers of this age understood it, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. It is revealed through the Spirit, who searches everything, even the depths of God. “No one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God.” We have received the Spirit, so that we might understand the gifts freely given to us.

“The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.” This explains why people without the Spirit find the gospel foolish. And the chapter ends with a wonderful statement: “But we have the mind of Christ.” By the Spirit, believers can think God’s thoughts after him through his word.
connection: Isaiah 29:14 and Jeremiah 9:23-24 are quoted in chapter 1. Acts 18:1-18 tells of the founding of the church. Isaiah 64:4 and 40:13 are quoted in chapter 2. Galatians 6:14 is a parallel boast in the cross. Philippians 2:1-11 speaks of the mind of Christ. John 16:13-15 promises the Spirit who guides into truth. Romans 1:16 and Colossians 2:2-3 speak of Christ as the center. 1 Peter 2:4-8 says Christ is a stone of stumbling. Ephesians 1:17-18 prays for the Spirit of wisdom.
application:
Ask if you are boasting in a leader, a ministry, or a tradition more than in Christ. Replace the boast.

Pray for the Spirit to illumine a passage as you read Scripture this week.

If you feel weak or foolish in the world’s eyes, remember that God chose the weak.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the foolishness of the cross that saves you.
Ask him to keep your eyes on Christ crucified.
Tell him where you are tempted to rely on human wisdom.
